prompt: Work out whether a class writes its own toString, and separately whether the toString it would actually use is anything better than Object's. Complete the starter file, then run the tests.
explanation: getDeclaredMethod looks only at the class you ask about and throws NoSuchMethodException when the method is not written there, which makes the try/catch the idiomatic way to phrase a does-this-exist question. getMethod searches the whole superclass chain for a public method, so it always succeeds for toString -- the useful information is getDeclaringClass(), which names the class that actually supplied it. Comparing that with Object.class is how debuggers and logging libraries decide whether printing an object is worth anything. The two answers come apart precisely when a class inherits an override rather than writing one.
hints: getDeclaredMethod("toString") takes no parameter types after the name because toString has no parameters.
A method that exists is reported by the call simply returning; a method that does not throws NoSuchMethodException, so return true in the try and false in the catch.
For the second method, getMethod always finds toString somewhere -- the question is whether method.getDeclaringClass() is Object.class.
